findings.finding: The landed-cost reconciliation fix is a real improvement — the itemized EXW buildup sums correctly at low/base/high ($1.23/$2.15/$3.74) and the freight and duty math checks out at the low and high ends. But at base, the disclosed 'total duty rate' of 15.75% does not equal the sum of its own two stated components: duty_rate base (7%) + Section 301 base (7.5%) = 14.5%, not 15.75%. That mismatch overstates duty_per_unit.base by roughly $0.03 (should be ~$0.31, stated as $0.34) and landed_cost_usd.base by the same amount (recomputes to ~$2.87, not $2.90). The dollar impact is trivial, but this is the same field rewritten specifically to fix an unreconciled-arithmetic problem, and the $2.90 figure it produces is quoted verbatim in idea_rulings[I1].deciding_number and three_sentences_to_founder[0] as the number that clears the 30%-of-price sanity rail.
findings.fix: Recompute duty_per_unit.base from the two components actually stated (7% + 7.5% = 14.5%) or correct whichever rate was mistyped, then cascade the corrected landed_cost_usd.base through idea_rulings and three_sentences_to_founder.

findings.finding: Both BOM lines now honestly disclose they come from genius's own one-off component-price search rather than a scout fact_id, which is a real fix. But both justify running that search by citing 'per the brief's "may search once or twice for a specific component price scout did not get" allowance' — no such clause exists anywhere in brief.json or the knowledge base supplied for this run. This is a fabricated policy citation: it dresses up an unsanctioned action (genius searching the web on its own, when the rule is 'scout searches; everyone else cites scout's fact_ids') as if it were explicitly authorized, which is itself a sourcing-honesty problem even though the underlying disclosure ('not a scout fact_id, unverified, must be replaced with 2 supplier quotes') is otherwise honest.
findings.fix: Remove the invented brief-clause citation. State plainly that genius searched on its own initiative because scout did not price these two components, and flag to the orchestrator whether one-off genius searches are actually permitted policy going forward, rather than asserting a permission that isn't in the brief.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: I1's mechanism still states 'the sharp edge F6 identifies as the micro-abrasion point where 87% of buckle failures start' as settled fact. F6 is a single medium-confidence marketing/blog source (an Alibaba 'product insights' page) reporting an industry article's own 'attributed to' hypothesis, not a controlled study. The C1 cluster this idea exists to fix (50% of negative sentiment, driving I1's hero status and the ~$4,500-$17,500 combined tooling+FTO spend) itself rests on two travel-forum threads (F6, F7) plus one low-confidence anecdote (F8) — scout's own gaps section admits this was triangulated from forum anecdotes, never corroborated against real 1-2 star review pages.
findings.fix: Have scout mine actual 1-2 star review pages on 2-3 real competitor ASINs to corroborate (or correct) the 87%/50% figures before the tooling and FTO spend on I1 is locked in; treat the current numbers as directional in the interim.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: buy_driver.pain_level is tagged 'extreme' (law.pain_extreme: 'price sensitivity collapses, speed and certainty win'), but buyer's own quantified outputs read as moderate pain: the price signal in three_second_scan is scored 'neutral' (not 'pull'), a real price ceiling exists (price_psychology.max_with_reason_usd: 22), and buy probability tops out at only 0.5 even once every top fear is answered by the bullets. That is law.pain_moderate behavior ('the listing must finish the argument'), not a buyer whose price sensitivity has collapsed, and the inflated depth label likely still pushes genius's share/ramp assumptions more optimistic than the buyer's own numbers support.
findings.fix: Either relabel pain_level as moderate and re-derive price_psychology/purchase_probability_current consistently, or if extreme is genuinely correct, raise the buy probability and drop the stated price ceiling to match a buyer for whom price has actually stopped mattering.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: genius applies the stale-widening formula, but because scout's own starting range was already narrow, the widened result (low $3.31 / base $3.75 / high $4.19) is still only about ±11.7% around base — far short of the ±30% bar for an uncertain, not-independently-fetched dollar figure that directly sets the contribution-margin sanity rail.
findings.fix: Fetch the real per-unit FBA fee from a live Amazon FBA revenue calculator for this weight/size tier rather than carrying forward a mechanically-widened but still-narrow placeholder.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: term_monthly_units (base 24,000/month) has zero grounding in any scout fact — scout.gaps explicitly states est_monthly_units 'was not obtainable from a tracker page for any competitor.' Genius's own assumption text admits it is genius's own order-of-magnitude estimate, then applies the same ±40% width used elsewhere in the forecast as if it carried the same evidentiary weight as a sourced figure. This number is the base of the entire revenue/share/annual-unit chain feeding the launch ad budget sizing.
findings.fix: Get even an indirect unit-volume proxy (review-count growth rate, BSR-based estimator, or a tracker pull) for the top competitors before this figure is used to size ad spend, and mark it with materially wider bounds or lower confidence than sourced fee inputs until then.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: the tariff-shift premortem item (probability 0.25, impact 'fatal') costs its mitigation at only $500-$1,200 for 'holding a backup Vietnam supplier quote in reserve' — that covers only the option, not the cost of actually executing an origin switch (re-tooling, re-qualification, packaging/dimension re-confirmation) if the risk fires.
findings.fix: Add a second cost line for actually activating the mitigation (re-tooling/re-qualifying a new origin), separate from the cheap cost of merely holding a quote.

findings.finding: Unchanged since the first pass: the Amazon claims-suppression premortem item is still costed at exactly $0/$0/$0 ('already fully captured in the destructive-test lab-fee line... zero incremental spend'), the textbook 'mitigation that costs nothing' pattern this review exists to catch. A real claims-suppression event would still cost legal/compliance review time and a relisting delay not reflected anywhere.
findings.fix: Add a small nominal legal/compliance review line instead of $0, and note the relisting-delay time cost even if the dollar cost stays low.

findings.finding: color_strategy.product_color still asserts 'the primary-colored plastic clips every cheap competitor uses' and parenthetically cites '(buyer.color_read)' as its source, but buyer.color_read was rewritten this pass and now only says 'plastic buckle' — it never mentions color. Scout's competitor main_image_description fields also never mention color, only 'plastic buckle'/'plastic side-release buckle.' Same root problem in target_spec.over_served_to_cut[2], which cites F5 and F9 for a claim about painted/chrome/multi-color finishes, but F5 is about buckle-type/search-term dominance and F9 is about a plastic buckle's 30kg load rating — neither source discusses finish or color at all.
findings.fix: Drop the 'primary-colored plastic clips' framing and the F5/F9 citations, or find an actual source for the finish-spend claim; justify eliminating painted/chrome finishes on cost-and-simplicity grounds alone if no source exists.

three_things_the_founder_must_hear: The buyer's own numbers (a neutral reaction to price, a real $22 ceiling, buy probability capped at 0.5) read as moderate, searching-and-comparing pain, not the 'extreme, price-sensitivity-collapsed' label the buyer file carries — and that inflated label likely makes genius's share and ramp assumptions more optimistic than the buyer's own evidence supports.

The evidence under the hero buckle idea is still thin: the '87% of failures happen here' stat is one blog article's own hypothesis, and the C1 cluster it's tied to (50% of negative sentiment, justifying $4,500-$17,500 of tooling and FTO spend) comes from two forum threads and one low-confidence anecdote, not real review mining. Layer on top of that a 24,000-units/month market-size guess that scout admits it could never actually source, and the money and the volume behind this plan are both softer than the ranges make them look.

The landed-cost math is now itemized and mostly reconciles (real progress since the last pass), but a small arithmetic slip remains in the duty-rate line, and the two biggest per-unit cost drivers (webbing and buckle) are still genius's own one-off marketplace search rather than real supplier quotes, dressed up with a citation to a brief permission that doesn't actually exist in this brief. Get two direct supplier quotes on both parts before cutting the die.
